title: Preventing falls at home
notes: Most falls happen at home, and most can be prevented. On every visit, look for loose rugs, cords, clutter, poor lighting and wet floors, and fix what you can. Make sure your client wears shoes or socks with grip. Remind them to sit up and stand up slowly, and to wait a moment before walking.
review_note: The Mayo Clinic list opens with reviewing medications with the doctor (not a caregiver task).

videos.title: Fall Prevention and Home Safety Tips
videos.why: Walks room by room through a real home pointing out trip hazards.

videos.title: Tips to Prevent Falls and Stay Independent as You Age
videos.why: Short federal overview of home safety changes and habits.

videos.title: Tips on preventing falls at home
videos.why: Shoes, lighting, clutter and taking your time.

title: After a fall: do not lift
flag: CC rule: never lift or help up a client who has fallen. Keep them comfortable on the floor, call 911 if they are hurt or you are not sure, and call the office every time.
notes: If your client falls, do not try to lift them or help them up, even if they ask. Stay with them, check for pain, bleeding or a bump on the head, and keep them comfortable and warm on the floor with a pillow and blanket. Call 911 if they are hurt or if you are not sure. Call the office every time, even if they seem fine.
review_note: Only one video fits your never-lift rule: nearly every other 'after a fall' video teaches helping the person up, so all were rejected. This one is told from a family member's view and says 'call hospice'; the notes say call the office. Could not confirm who runs the Eden channel. A short video of you explaining the rule may serve better.

videos.publisher: Hospice and Palliative Care with Eden (hospice staff member)
videos.why: Says plainly 'I cannot lift her up', checks her, gives a pillow and blanket, looks for a head bump, calls for help.

title: Using a gait belt
notes: A gait belt gives you a safe, steady place to hold so you never pull on your client's arms or clothes. Put it snug around the waist, over clothing, with room for two fingers underneath. Hold it from behind or the side with an underhand grip while they stand and walk. Take it off when you are done.
review_note: EquipMeOT's description links to products it sells. Rejected a Hospice Care Plan gait belt video because the client hugs the caregiver around the shoulders.

title: Bed to chair: the stand-pivot transfer
notes: Before you move anyone, lock the wheelchair brakes, move the footrests out of the way, and put the chair close and at an angle. Have your client scoot forward with feet flat, put on the gait belt, and count to three together. Let them push up with their own arms, turn with small steps, and lower them slowly until they feel the seat. If they cannot bear weight, stop and call the office.
review_note: The Open RN video is set in a facility; the skill is the same at home.

title: Walkers and canes
notes: A walker or cane only helps if it is used the right way. The handle should be about wrist height when your client's arms hang down. Their cane goes in the hand opposite the weak leg. When you walk with them, stay close on their weaker side, a little behind, and use a gait belt if they need hands-on help.
review_note: These are aimed at the person using the device, not the caregiver. AskDoctorJo is a clinician's own channel.

title: Wheelchair safety
notes: Lock both brakes every time your client gets in or out of the wheelchair. Use the footrests when you push so feet do not drag, and ask them to keep their hands in their lap through doorways. Go slowly on ramps and curbs, and never hang heavy bags on the back handles, because the chair can tip.
review_note: The first video is British.

videos.why: Footwear, blankets away from wheels, ramps, doorways, curbs and talking to the rider.

title: Getting in and out of a car
notes: Push the car seat all the way back and open the door wide first. Have your client back up until they feel the seat behind their legs, sit down first, then swing their legs in. Protect their head from the door frame. Never let them pull on the car door, because it moves.
review_note: Handicare ends with a short sales plug for a swivel cushion. Left out a Singapore hospital video that says 'lift them'.

title: Shower and tub safety (transfer bench, grab bars)
notes: The bathroom is where many falls happen. Before a shower, put a non-slip mat in the tub and a dry mat outside it, and have towels and clothes within reach. Your client should sit on the shower chair or transfer bench and hold grab bars, never towel racks. Check the water temperature first and stay close the whole time.

title: Protecting your back
notes: Your back has to last your whole career, so protect it on every move. Stand close, feet apart, knees bent and back straight, and let your legs do the work. Turn your feet instead of twisting your body. If a move feels like too much for one person, stop and call the office.
review_note: The FCA video says 'lift' in places; it does not show lifting someone off the floor.

title: Mechanical (Hoyer) lift
flag: Medicaid clients: any lift transfer is an advanced personal care task a nurse must certify. CC does not offer it, so a Medicaid client who needs a lift is flagged to the office, not matched. Private pay: only when the care plan says so.
notes: A Hoyer lift is only used when your client's care plan says so, and only after the office has trained you on that client's lift and sling. Always follow the lift maker's instructions, use the right sling for that lift, and check the straps and hooks before every lift.

title: Giving a bed bath
notes: A bed bath is for someone who can't safely get to the tub or shower. Keep them covered, keep the room warm, and only uncover the part you are washing. Go from cleanest to dirtiest, and look at the skin as you go. Tell the office about any red spots, sores or rashes.

title: Helping with a shower
notes: Get everything ready before they undress: towels, soap, clean clothes and the shower chair. Check the water on your own wrist first. Let them sit and do as much as they can for themselves. Keep a towel over them so they don't feel exposed.

title: Mouth care and dentures
notes: Clean teeth twice a day, using a soft brush and gentle strokes. If they wear dentures, take them out and clean them over a sink lined with a towel so they won't break if dropped. Store them in water in their own labeled cup. Tell the office about any mouth sores, bleeding or pain.

title: Dressing someone with a weak side
notes: When one side is weak, remember: dress the weak side first, and undress the strong side first. Move the weak arm or leg gently and never pull or twist it. Let them help with the strong side as much as they can.
review_note: The LACC video is a state-exam skill demo, so it looks staged. Unique Senior Care may be a UK provider ('carer').

title: Shaving, hair and grooming
notes: An electric razor is the safest choice, especially for anyone on blood thinners. Ask how they like their hair and face done, and let them look in the mirror. If they can't get to the sink, you can wash their hair in bed with a basin and towels.
review_note: Could not tell if 'Helping Someone Shave' uses a blade razor; check before approving. Whether CC caregivers may use blade razors is your rule to set (the notes only say electric is safest).

title: Changing a brief standing up
notes: If they can stand with support, have them hold a grab bar, counter or walker while you work. Wear gloves, clean front to back, and check the skin for redness. Talk them through each step so they know what's coming. If they get tired or wobbly, help them sit right away.

title: Handwashing and gloves
notes: Wash your hands when you arrive, before and after personal care, and before you leave. Scrub for at least 20 seconds, including between your fingers and under your nails. Put on fresh gloves for each task. Take them off so the dirty side folds inward, then wash your hands again.

title: Signs of a urinary tract infection
notes: In older adults, a UTI often doesn't look like a UTI. The first sign may be new confusion, more falls, sleepiness or acting unlike themselves. You might also notice strong-smelling or cloudy urine, or more accidents than usual. Report any sudden change to the office the same day. Don't wait for it to pass.
review_note: No strong short video from a top publisher. CarDon is a company channel; the UC Irvine video is 26 minutes. Watch both for treatment or medication talk.

videos.title: Understanding UTIs in Seniors: Symptoms, Treatment & Prevention Tips for Elderly Health
videos.publisher: CarDon & Associates (Indiana senior living), with a nurse practitioner
videos.why: UTIs in older adults often show up as confusion, agitation, falls or mood change.

title: Helping someone drink enough
notes: Older adults often don't feel thirsty, so they can get dehydrated without noticing. Watch for dark urine, dry mouth, dizziness, constipation or new confusion. Offer small drinks often and drink with them. Try foods with lots of water, like soup or fruit. If the care plan limits fluids, follow the plan. Tell the office if they are drinking very little.
review_note: Dementia Careblazers is a clinician's own channel, not an organization.

videos.why: Short, clear list of dehydration signs in older adults.

videos.why: Eight practical tips to encourage fluids.

title: Safe swallowing and choking signs
notes: Some clients have trouble swallowing, and food or drink can go down the wrong way. Always help your client sit fully upright to eat and for at least 30 minutes after. Offer small bites and sips, and go slow. If you see coughing, choking, a wet or gurgly voice, or watery eyes during meals, call the office right away, and call 911 if they cannot breathe or speak.
review_note: KTPH is a Singapore hospital, so accents and some terms are non-US. Gaylord 'What is Dysphagia' is optional third pick; drop it if you want only two.

title: Thickened liquids
notes: If your client's care plan says thickened liquids, every drink must be thickened, including water, coffee, and juice. Use the exact level the plan says, like mildly thick or moderately thick. Follow the directions on the thickener can for how much to use, stir well, and let it sit the time it says. Never give a thin drink to someone who needs thickened ones.
review_note: Gaylord video may use older terms (nectar-thick, honey-thick) next to IDDSI levels. The Chesterfield video is UK and uses a UK thickener brand; scoop amounts differ by brand, so caregivers must follow the label on the client's own product. The IDDSI flow test needs a 10 mL syringe; decide whether you want caregivers doing it.

title: Soft, minced and pureed food
notes: Some clients need softer food so they can swallow safely. Your client's care plan will say which level, such as soft and bite-sized, minced and moist, or pureed. Make the food match that level every time, with no hard bits, skins, or dry crumbs. Pureed food can still look nice: puree each food separately, keep the colors apart on the plate, and add a little sauce or gravy for flavor.
review_note: None of the strongest picks focus mainly on making puree look appetizing; that tip is covered in the notes. Product-pitch puree videos were excluded.

title: Diabetic meals and low blood sugar
notes: For clients with diabetes, follow the meal plan in their care plan. A simple guide is the plate: half vegetables, a quarter protein, and a quarter starch or fruit, with water or a sugar-free drink. Watch for low blood sugar signs like shaking, sweating, confusion, or acting unlike themselves, and for high blood sugar signs like extreme thirst, peeing a lot, or unusual tiredness. Follow the client's care plan, call the office, and call 911 if they pass out or cannot swallow.
review_note: The low blood sugar video may mention glucagon or medication; caregivers must not give it. Watch it and decide, or swap in Rapides Regional 'Dish on Diabetes - The 15:15 Rule' (youtube.com/watch?v=OoiX6jx48L8, nurse educator) if your care plans use the 15-15 rule.

title: Low-salt cooking (heart failure, blood pressure)
notes: Many clients with heart failure or high blood pressure need less salt, so follow the limit in their care plan. When you shop, check the label for sodium and pick low-sodium or no-salt-added foods. Cook with herbs, lemon, garlic, and pepper instead of salt, and go easy on canned soups, deli meat, and frozen dinners. Tell the office if you notice new swelling in the feet or legs, fast weight gain, or more trouble breathing.
review_note: The heart failure videos may briefly mention fluid limits or medicines; caregivers follow the care plan only.

title: Kidney (renal) diet basics
notes: Clients with kidney disease often have limits on salt, potassium, phosphorus, and sometimes how much they drink. These limits are different for each person, so always follow your client's own care plan and don't guess. Foods like bananas, potatoes, oranges, tomatoes, dairy, and dark colas can be high in potassium or phosphorus. If your client has a fluid limit, help them track it, and tell the office about swelling, shortness of breath, or fast weight gain.
review_note: The fluid video is aimed at dialysis patients; only keep it if you have dialysis clients.

title: Helping someone eat
notes: When you help someone eat, sit down at their eye level, not standing over them. Let them do as much as they can on their own, and use special spoons, cups, or plates if they have them. Give small bites, wait until each bite is swallowed, and talk with them like it's a normal meal. For clients with dementia, keep it calm and simple, offer one food at a time, and use gentle cues.

title: Poor appetite and weight loss
notes: Many older adults lose their appetite, and losing weight without trying can be a sign that something is wrong. Offer small meals and snacks often instead of three big meals, and serve foods they like. Eating together, a pleasant setting, and something to drink nearby can help. Tell the office if your client is eating much less, skipping meals, has clothes getting loose, or seems weaker.

title: Talking with someone who has dementia
notes: Always come from the front, slowly, so the person sees you before you get close. Say their name, smile, and use short, simple words. If they say something that is not true, do not argue or correct them. Go along with their feelings and gently guide them to something else.

title: Sundowning, wandering and distress
notes: Many people with dementia get more upset or restless in the late afternoon and evening. Keep the day calm and on a routine, turn on lights before dark, and offer a snack, a drink, or a walk. If they want to leave, do not block or argue, go with them and gently redirect. If they leave the home and you cannot find them, call 911 right away, then call the office.

title: Bathing and personal care with dementia
notes: Bathing can feel cold, scary, and embarrassing for someone with dementia. Get everything ready first, keep the room warm, and keep them covered with a towel. Use Hand-under-Hand so they feel in control, and go one small step at a time. If they say no, stop, wait a bit, and try again later or another way.

title: Helping someone with Parkinson's
notes: People with Parkinson's can suddenly freeze, as if their feet are stuck to the floor. Never pull or push them. Stay calm and give a simple cue, like counting out loud, marching in place, or stepping over a line on the floor. Clear clutter and rugs, and watch closely during turns and doorways, where falls happen most. If they fall, do not lift them. Keep them comfortable, call 911 if they are hurt, and call the office.

title: Caring for someone after a stroke
notes: After a stroke, one side of the body may be weak, and the person may not notice things on that side. Stand on their weak side when you help them walk, and put things where they can see them. If talking is hard for them, speak slowly, ask yes or no questions, and give them time to answer. If you see new stroke signs, like a drooping face or new weakness, call 911 right away.

title: Oxygen safety at home
flag: Never change the oxygen setting. Only the client's nurse or doctor changes it.
notes: Oxygen makes fire burn very fast. Never allow smoking, candles, gas stoves, or open flames near the oxygen, and keep it at least 10 feet away from heat. Keep tubing out of walkways so no one trips. Never change the oxygen setting yourself. If something seems wrong with the machine or their breathing, call the office, and call 911 if they are struggling to breathe.
review_note: The American Lung Association video is aimed at patients and may talk about flow rate; drop it if it suggests changing settings.

title: Heart failure: signs to report
notes: With heart failure, small changes can mean the body is holding fluid. Write down their weight at the same time each morning if that is in the care plan. Call the office if they gain 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, or if you see new swelling, more coughing, or more trouble breathing when lying down. Call 911 for chest pain, severe trouble breathing, or fainting.
review_note: The 2-3 lb / 5 lb thresholds are common AHA guidance; check against your care-plan wording.

title: COPD and shortness of breath
notes: When someone with COPD gets short of breath, help them sit up, lean forward a little, and breathe in through the nose and out slowly through pursed lips. Plan the day so hard tasks are spread out, with rests in between. Call the office if they are more breathless than usual, coughing more, or the mucus changes color. Call 911 if they cannot catch their breath, are confused, or their lips turn blue or gray.

title: When to call the office or 911
notes: You know your client best, so trust yourself when something seems different. If they seem less alert, eat or drink less, are weaker, or just are not acting like themselves, call the office right away. Call 911 first for stroke signs (BE FAST), chest pain, trouble breathing, a bad fall, or sudden confusion, then call the office.
review_note: AHA teaches F.A.S.T., UC San Diego teaches BE FAST; pick one for a single message. Stop and Watch was made for nursing homes but carries over.

title: Spotting infection early in older adults
notes: Older adults often do not get a fever when they have an infection. Instead, you may see new confusion, more sleepiness, weakness, falls, not eating, or changes when they use the bathroom. These changes can come on fast, so call the office the same day you notice them. Call 911 if they are very hard to wake, struggling to breathe, or seem very sick.
